entries.text: At 0230 I keyed the corridor timing override myself, gloves off so the panel would read my prints as routine maintenance.
The outer seal made a low double knock when the cycle shifted, like a fist on a hatch, and I stood there listening to it longer than I should have.
I had memorized Lena's walk-through schedule for weeks; she always cut through Sector C at the end of the audit prep, alone, between 0250 and 0310.
Two hours after the breach I rewrote the resource ledger entries, moving the diverted allocations under decommissioned storage codes.
When Lena announced the audit I felt my hands go cold; the diversion trail led straight to my console and she was three queries away from it.
I keep telling myself the lower decks are alive because of what I moved, that one death bought forty breathing people, and some nights I almost believe it.
The diverted oxygen cells sit behind a false manifest in Bay Nine; I sign for their inspection myself so no one else ever opens the crate.
The last thing Lena ever said to me was that numbers don't lie but people do, and she smiled when she said it, like she already knew.
I made myself join the response team and I saw her through the port glass, and I have not slept a full cycle since.
Every time the detective pauses before a question I am certain the next word will be the ledger codes, and I rehearse my calm face in the silence.
I ran the pressure cascade twice in simulation on my private slate, deleted the runs, and then wiped the slate's recovery partition anyway.
In the dream the corridor door is transparent and Lena watches me key the override, and she is not angry, which is worse.
My sister Mara breathes through a filtered line on the medical deck, and I check her oxygen draw numbers every morning before I eat.
When command cut the medical reserve quota last winter, Mara's line pressure dropped for six hours, and I decided then that the ledgers belonged to me, not to them.
Most mornings I walk the spine corridor with a thermal scanner and coffee gone cold, reading the bulkhead joints like other people read the news.
I have rebuilt the Sector C intake valves so many times I can feel a worn gasket through the wrench before the gauge shows anything.
This station was built for eight hundred people and holds twelve hundred, and the fact that anyone breathes at all is engineering, not luck.
Command writes policy memos about efficiency from the upper ring, where the air recyclers are new and the water never tastes of iron.
Lena Voss was the only director who ever learned the difference between a pressure fault and a sensor fault, and she checked my work like she meant it.
Nine years ago a dorm section vented on the old ring and we sealed it with foam and prayer; I carried two people out and one of them still sends me solstice cards.
The lower deck families hang wet laundry across the service catwalks, and I pretend not to see it because their dehumidifiers were rationed out two winters ago.
From the observation dome the sunrise crosses the solar arrays in a slow gold line, and the whole station hums half a tone higher as the panels warm.
The canteen serves protein loaf on third-days and I eat it at the same corner table, back to the wall, watching the pressure telltales over the door.
The night before the breach I stood outside the records office for ten minutes with a data spike in my pocket, and then walked away because the corridor plan was already better.
My father's torque driver hangs above my bunk; the handle is worn to the shape of a hand that was bigger than mine.
I logged a diagnostic session at my console for the whole incident window; the session ran on a script I wrote to touch a key every ninety seconds.
Lena and I argued once in front of the whole operations floor about shutting down Bay Nine circulation, and she won, because she always won on paper.
Twice I have opened a blank message to the safety board and typed the first sentence of a confession, and twice I deleted it and ran corridor diagnostics until my hands stopped.
Sector C smells of ozone and old coolant, and the lights above junction twelve flicker in a pattern maintenance has never once reproduced on demand.
The junior engineers bring me their mistakes before they bring them to the log, and I fix most of them quietly, because that is how you keep people honest.
During the incident window I sat in the pump room with the lights off, counting seal cycles by sound, and when the alarm finally came I was already standing.
People here still talk about weather that no one has felt in years; we call solar flare season winter and pretend the word means something.
The one thing I could not control is the corridor's own timing buffer, which keeps a rolling shadow log somewhere in the safety core that I have no access to.
My quarters share a wall with the number four air handler, and after twenty years its bearing noise is the only thing that reliably puts me to sleep.
In our last scheduled meeting Lena spread the allocation printouts across my bench and tapped three lines with her pen, and I explained two of them well.
I did the arithmetic a hundred times: expose the diversion and the lower decks lose their margin inside a quarter; lose Lena and the numbers stay buried; I chose the arithmetic.

My statement to the investigation is on record: I spent the whole incident window at my console in the engineering bay running a corridor diagnostic, and the session log confirms it keystroke by keystroke.
